title: Co-registration of mouse cortical structures between in vivo and ex vivo images using tangential sectioning
protocol: Capture a widefield image showing the surface vasculature pattern of the entire cranial window.
Thaw and inject 30 μl of diluted dextran solution subcutaneously under skin on the back without anesthesia, using a syringe with 31G needle.
Perform functional two-photon calcium imaging of the cortical structures of interest.
Set emission filter for GCaMP to 470–588 nm.
Set emission filter for dextran-Texas Red to 600–722 nm.
Use Nikon 16× 0.8NA objective.
After functional imaging, without moving the XY position of the objective, record a two-photon z-stack with both GCaMP and dextran channels.
Ensure visibility of 3D vasculature pattern and structures of interest in the stack.
Set starting depth to ∼10 μm above highest point of pia surface.
Set ending depth to 500 μm below pia surface or 100 μm below the structure of interest.
Set Z-Step depth to 4 μm.
Average 100 frames per step.
Optionally, without moving the XY position of the objective, record a surface two-photon z-stack in both channels with the largest field of view possible.
Set starting depth for optional recording to ∼10 μm above highest point of pia surface.
Set ending depth for optional recording to 100 μm below pia surface.
Set Z-Step depth for optional recording to 10 μm.
Average 100 frames per step for optional recording.
Save the mean projection of the stack as two-photon surface vasculature pattern for optional recording.

Optionally, without moving the XY position of the objective, record a local widefield surface vasculature stack through the same objective if it has larger field of view than the two-photon field of view.
Set starting depth for this step to ∼10 μm above highest point of pia surface.
Record ending depth at where the surface vasculature pattern is defocused.
Set Z-Step depth for this step to 10 μm.
Capture 1 image per step.
Save the mean projection of the stack as local wide-field surface vasculature pattern.
Perfuse 10 mL saline through the circulatory system at a flow rate of 9 mL/min or until the liver is clear under anesthesia.
Perfuse with 50 mL of freshly prepared 4% PFA at a flow rate of 9 mL/min.
Extract the brain and immerse it in 4% PFA at 20°C–25°C for 3–6 hours.
Immerse the brain in 4% PFA at 4°C for 12–24 hours.
After fixation, immerse the brain in 1× PBS with 0.01% sodium azide at 4°C in the dark for long-term storage (up to one year).
Take the fixed brain out of PBS + 0.01% sodium azide.
Gently press the flattened area of cortex facing down against a clean glass slide.
Ensure the flattened area is fully in contact with the glass.
Place a metal ring around the brain and rest it on top of the glass slide to create a mold.
Carefully pour warmed liquid agarose into the mold to embed the brain.
Ensure the cortical surface is flat against the glass slide.
Pour the agarose to the top of the mold to prevent unevenness and bubbles.
Wait until the agarose has cooled to approximately 40°C before proceeding.
Place another glass slide on top of the metal ring after pouring the agarose.
Place a weight (100 g or similar) on top of this slide to ensure it stays in contact with the metal ring.
Solidify the agarose.
Gently push out the agarose block from the ring onto a glass slide.
Trim one round edge of the agarose cylinder with a razor blade on the side where cutting would begin.
Glue the trimmed agarose block to the vibratome stage with the trimmed side facing the blade.
Position the agarose cylinder with the flat cortex side up and the trimmed side facing the blade.
Affix the agarose to the vibratome stage with a thin layer of super glue.
Fill the chamber with PBS just below the surface of the agarose cylinder.
Set the blade advancing speed at 0.21 mm/s.
Set the blade vibration frequency at 90 Hz.
Set cutting depth to a small increment such as 50 μm.
Slowly lower the blade step by step until it is barely cutting the agarose across the full width of the cylinder.
Stop the blade before it reaches the brain tissue to establish the zero position for sectioning.
From the zero position, with the blade fully retracted, lower the blade to the desired depth, e.g., 350 μm.
Fill the chamber with more PBS so the agarose is completely submerged and cut the first brain section.
Place tangential sections into 8% SDS in PBS at 37°C on a shaker for two days, then rinse in PBS five times for 5 min each (optional antigen retrieval step).
Rinse sections on a shaker in PBS 5 times for 5 minutes each if antigen retrieval was not performed.
Place tissue in blocking buffer NDSTU on a shaker at 20°C–25°C for 1 hour.
Incubate tissue for 2 days on a shaker at 20°C–25°C in primary antibody working solution.
Rinse tissue on a shaker at least 5 times for 5 minutes each in PBST.
Incubate tissue for 2 days on a shaker at 20°C–25°C in secondary antibody working solution.
Rinse tissue on a shaker 5 times for 5 minutes in PBST, then 5 times for 5 minutes in PBS.
Place the tissue into CUBIC-1 solution for ∼30 min at 20°C–25°C.
Create a chamber for the section by stacking spacers on a glass slide up to an appropriate height, e.g., 350 μm or 400 μm.
Mount the section and fill the chamber with 100 μL CUBIC-1 solution.
Apply a cover glass on top of the chamber slowly without creating any bubbles.
Seal the edges with clear nail polish.
Post process the tiled confocal depth stacks using TeraStitcher or compatible software.
Align and stitch all surface images and image volumes into a standard orientation.
Compare the in vivo widefield surface image with the ex vivo confocal surface overview to locate matching major blood vessels.
Locate the two-photon field of view in the widefield surface image.
Match the in vivo two-photon field of view to the ex vivo confocal surface image.
Move down through the cortical depth in both in vivo two-photon and ex vivo confocal volumes simultaneously.
Keep track of matching descending blood vessels as you move through the depths.
Continue moving until the target depth is reached.
Search for corresponding neuronal structures labeled by GCaMP in the green channel.
Identify matching blood vessels from surface to targeted region if possible.
Use unique shape or distribution pattern to identify brain structures with naked eye.
Generate and compare stepped z projections every 50 μm using FIJI software when necessary.
Find the corresponding entity (e.g., soma, spine, bouton) in both volumes.
Extract functional characteristics of the entity from in vivo calcium activity recorded by two-photon imaging.
